To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ethanol docks onto an alcohol recognition site strategically positioned between the BK channel calcium-sensors and pore gate, and that ethanol only accesses this site when the BK channel’s endogenous agonist calcium is present.
we identified and characterized a novel ethanol recognition site in BK (slo) channel-forming proteins.

(i) we have identified an alcohol-recognition site in the BK channel; (ii) this alcohol-recognition site is located in proximity to the BK channel’s calcium-sensors and is accessible in presence of calcium; (iii) ethanol interacts with the BK channel through a water-accessible, polar site; (iv) ethanol hydrogen bonds to a single residue, K361, located at the BK channel’s ethanol-recognition site; and (v) substitutions that hamper ethanol hydrogen bond formation
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular determinants that underlie the interaction between BK channels and ethanol, a widely consumed and abused drug.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of ethanol on the large-conductance calcium- and voltage-activated potassium (BK) ion channel.

understanding the mechanism by which ethanol interacts with the BK channel and how this mechanism can be used to design agents that block ethanol’s actions on BK channels without perturbing channel function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we identified and characterized the first ethanol-recognition site in the BK channel.
this work identifies and characterizes an n-alkanols recognition site in the BK channel, a member of the TM6 superfamily of voltage- and ligand-gated channels.
the present study presents the first identification and functional characterization of an alcohol recognition site in a voltage-gated ion channel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified and characterized an alcohol recognition site in the large conductance potassium channel (BK).
we identified and characterized the first alcohol-sensing site (ASS) in the voltage-gated calcium- and voltage-dependent, large conductance, potassium (BK) ion channel.
we identified and characterized an alcohol recognition site within the BK channel that is strategically positioned to modulate channel activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the alcohol-sensing site is located at the interface between the slo1 voltage sensor and the calcium-sensors.
we have discovered and characterized an alcohol-sensing, allosteric site in BK channels.
we have identified the first alcohol-sensing site within a voltage/calcium-activated potassium channel and that this site is located in the channel’s cytoplasmic vestibule.
